readings.c2s3:
¶
{{smaller block|After a grindstone . . . has been used for a time in sharpening chisels, the surface gets a dark metallic glaze, and the stone will not then bite the steel. To remove this glaze the stone was ''whetted'' or sharpened (both terms were used) by rubbing it with sand and water, the rubbing medium being a piece of stone harder . . . and of coarser grain.|{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 173.}}}}

'''4.''' To prune or preen; trim. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>There, like a bird, it sits and sings,
Then ''whets'' and claps its silver wings.</poem>
{{right|''Marvell'', The Garden.}}}}

'''5.''' To cut with a knife. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''To whet on''' or '''whet forward†''', to urge on; instigate.
{{smaller block|<poem>I prithee, peace, good queen,
And ''whet'' not ''on'' these furious peers.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 34.}}}}

'''To whet one’s whistle†.''' Same as ''to wet one’s whistle'' (confusion of ''wet'' and ''whet''). See ''whistle.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Give the boy some drink there! Piper,
''Whet your whistle.'' ''Fletcher'', Beggars’ Bush, iii. 1.</poem>
Let ’s e’en say grace, and turn to the fire, drink the other cup to ''whet our whistles'', and so sing away all sad thoughts.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 86.}}}}

'''whet''' (hwet), ''n.'' [< ''whet'', ''v.''] The act of sharpening by friction; hence, something that provokes or stimulates; especially, something that whets the appetite, as a dram.
{{smaller block|You are cloy’d with the Preparative, and what you mean for a ''Whet'' turns the Edge of your puny Stomachs.
{{right|''Congreve'', Old Batchelor, i. 4.}}}}

{{RunningHeader|whereunder|6895|whether}}Shone resurgent, a sunbright sign, Through shapes ''whereunder'' the strong soul glows. {{smaller block|{{right|''Swinburne'', Death of W. Bell Scott.}}}} '''whereuntil''' (hwãr-un-til′), ''conj.''   [< ''where''1 + ''until.'']   Whereunto. [Obsolete or provincial.] {{smaller block|We know ''whereuntil'' it doth amount. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 493.}}}} '''whereunto†''' (hwãr-un′tö or -un-tö′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ''where''1 + ''unto.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Unto what or whom? whereto? {{smaller block|''Whereunto'' shall we liken the kingdom of God? {{right|Mark iv. 30.}}}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' To which or whom; unto what; for what end or purpose. {{smaller block|Now when Andrew heard ''whereunto'' Christ was come, he forsook his master John, and came to Christ. {{right|''Latimer.''}}}} {{smaller block|The next ''whereunto.'' {{right|''Hooker.''}}}} '''whereupon''' (hwãr-u-pon′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wherupon''; < ''where''1 + ''upon.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Upon what place, ground, cause, etc.? whereon? '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Upon which or whom; whereon. {{smaller block|There [at the Mount of Olives] is Also the stone ''wher vpon'' the Aungell stod comfortyng hym the same tyme. {{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 28.}}}} {{smaller block|The king hath sent to know The nature of your griefs, and ''whereupon'' You conjure from the breast of civil peace Such bold hostility. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 42.}}}} {{smaller block|This was cast upon the board; . . . ''whereupon'' Rose feud, with question unto whom ’t were due. {{right|''Tennyson'', Œnone.}}}} '''wherever''' (hwãr-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wher evere''; < ''where''1 + ''ever.'']   At whatever place. {{smaller block|He hathe alweys 3 Wifes with him, ''where'' that ''evere'' he be. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 218.}}}} {{smaller block|They courted merit, ''wherever'' it was to be found. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 26.}}}} '''wherewith''' (hwãr-wiᴛ̵ʜ′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wherwith'', ''wharwith'', ''hwer with''; < ''where''1 + ''with''1.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' With what or whom? {{smaller block|O my Lord, ''wherewith'' shall I save Israel? Judges vi. 15.}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' With which; also, as compound relative, that with which. {{smaller block|And bisily gan for the soules preye [pray] Of hem that yaf him ''wherwith'' to scoleye [study]. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 302.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wherewith'' he fixt his eyes Vppon her fearefull face. {{right|''Gascoigne'', Philomene (Steele Glas, etc., ed. Arber, p. 96).}}}} {{smaller block|The love ''wherewith'' thou hast loved me. John xvii. 26.}} {{smaller block|Reverence is that ''wherewith'' princes are girt from God. {{right|''Bacon'', Seditions and Troubles (ed. 1887).}}}} {{smaller block|Was I in a desert, I would find out ''wherewith'' in it to call forth my affections. {{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, p. 29.}}}} {{smaller block|[''Wherewith'' is colloquially used as a noun in the phrase ''the wherewith'' (compare the commoner equivalent phrase ''the wherewithal'')—that is, what is necessary or required; means.}} {{smaller block|His [the Esquimaux’s] digestive system, heavily taxed in providing ''the wherewith'' to meet excessive loss by radiation, supplies less material for other purposes. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 15.]}}}} '''wherewithal''' (hwãr-wi-ᴛ̵ʜâl′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ''where''1 + ''withal''.]   Same as ''wherewith''. {{smaller block|''Wherewithal'' shall a young man cleanse his way? {{right|Ps. cxix. 9.}}}} {{smaller block|We our selves have not ''wherwithal''; who shall bear the Charges of our Journey? {{right|''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.}}}} {{smaller|'''The wherewithal.''' Same as ''the wherewith.'' See note under ''wherewith.'' [Colloq.]}} {{smaller block|For ''the wherewithal'' To give his babes a better bringing-up. {{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}} '''wherr''' (hwėr), ''a.''   [Prob. < W. ''chwerw'', bitter, sharp, severe; cf. ''chwerwon'', bitters, ''chwerwi'', become bitter. Cf. ''wherry''2.]   Very sour. [Prov. Eng.] '''wherret†, wherrit†''' (hwer′et, hwer′it), ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''whirret.'' '''wherry1''' (hwer′i), ''n.''; pl. ''wherries'' (-iz).   [Early mod. E. also ''whery'', ''whirrie'', ''whyrry''; origin unknown. According to Skeat, < Icel. ''hverfr'', shifty, crank (said of ships) (= Norw. ''kverv'', crank, unsteady, also swift), < ''hverfa'' (pret. ''hvarf''), turn: see ''wharf.'']   '''1.''' A light shallow rowboat, having seats for passengers, and plying on rivers and harbors. It resembles the dory. {{smaller block|A ''whyrry'', boate, ponto. {{right|''Levins'', Manip. Vocab., p. 106.}}}} {{smaller block|What sights of fine folks he oft row’d in his ''wherry'', ’Twas clean’d out so nice, and so painted withal. {{right|''C. Dibdin'', The Waterman.}}}} '''2.''' A light half-decked fishing-vessel used in different parts of Great Britain and Ireland. '''wherry2''' (hwer′i), ''n.''   [Cf. ''wherr.'']   A liquor made from the pulp of crab-apples after the verjuice is expressed. Sometimes called ''crab-wherry.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''wherryman''' (hwer′i-ma̤n), ''n.''; pl. ''wherrymen'' (-men). One who rows a wherry. {{smaller block|He that is an excellent ''wherryman'' looketh towards the bridge when he pulleth towards Westminster. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''wherso†''', ''indef. pron.''   [< ME. ''wherso'', contracted form of ''whetherso''.]   Same as ''whetherso''. Al is yliche good to me, Joye or sorowe, ''wherso'' it be. {{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 10.}}}} '''wherve†''', ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''wherven'', ''wherfen'', ''hwerfen'', < AS. ''hwerfan'', ''hwyrfan'' (pret. ''hwyrfde'') = OHG. ''hwerban'', ''hwarban'', ''werban'', ''werben'', MHG. ''werben'' = Icel. ''hverfa'', tr. cause to turn, turn, intr. turn, revolve; a weak verb, causative of early ME. *''hwerfen'' (in comp. ''a-hwerfen''), < AS. ''hweorfan'' (pret. ''hwearf'', pl. ''hwurfon'', pp. ''hworfen''), turn, turn about, go, = OS. ''hwerbhan'' = OFries. ''hwerva'', ''werva'', ''warfa'' = OHG. ''hwerban'', ''werban'', ''wervan'', ''werben'', MHG. ''werben'', ''werven'' = Icel. ''hverfa'' = Goth. ''hwairban'', turn, go about. This verb, lost in early ME., survives only in the derivatives ''wherve'', ''n.'', ''wharf'', ''whirl'', ''whorl'', etc.]   To turn; change. {{smaller block|Alfred . . . wrat tha laȝen on Englis, . . .
And ''whærfde'' hir nome on his and tornde the name in his daiȝe. {{right|''Layamon'', l. 6319.}}}} '''wherve''' (hwėrv), ''n.''   [Also ''wharve''; < ''wherve'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A round piece of wood put on a spindle to receive the thread. {{smaller block|Wouldst thou . . . blunt the spindles, join the ''wherves'', slander the spinning-quills, . . . of the weird Sister-Parcæ? {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 28.}}}} {{smaller block|So fine, so round, and even a thread she [the spider] spinnes, hanging thereunto herselfe, and using the weight of her own bodie instead of a ''wherve''. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xi. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|The spindle and ''wharve'' are rigidly attached to each other, and the upper section of the ''wharve'' is hollowed out to form a chamber capable of containing quite a quantity of oil. {{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXI. 342.}}}} '''2.''' A joint.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''whet''' (hwet), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''whetted'' or ''whet'', ppr. ''whetting''.   [< ME. ''whetten'', < AS. ''hwettan'' (= D. LG. ''wetten'' = OHG. ''wezzen'', MHG. G. ''wetzen'' = Icel. ''hvetja'' = Sw. ''hvässa'' = Dan. ''hvæsse''), sharpen, whet, < ''hwæt'', sharp: see ''what''2.]   '''1.''' To make sharp; sharpen (an edged or pointed tool or weapon) by rubbing it on a stone, or with an implement of stone or other material. {{smaller block|Assaying how hire speres weren ''whette.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1760.}}}} {{smaller block|I ''whette'' a knyfe, or any weapen or toole, to make it sharpe. . . . I love better ''whettynge'' of knyves afore a good dyner than ''whettynge'' of swordes and bylles. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 780.}}}} {{smaller block|And Beauty walkèd up and down With bow in hand, and arrows ''whet.'' {{right|''Lord Vaux'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 75).}}}} {{smaller block|And the mower ''whets'' his sithe. {{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 66.}}}} '''2.''' To make sharp, keen, or eager; excite; stimulate: as, to ''whet'' the appetite. {{smaller block|Since Cassius first did ''whet'' me against Cæsar, I have not slept. ''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 61.}} {{smaller block|The favourers of this fatal war, Whom this example did more sharply ''whet.'' {{right|''Drayton'', Barons’ Wars, iv. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|It but ''whets'' my stomach, which is too sharp-set already. {{right|''Middleton'', Chaste Maid, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Malice ''whets'' her sland’rous tongue. {{right|''Cowper'', Love Increased by Suffering.}}}} '''3.''' To rub; scratch.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|After a grindstone . . . has been used for a time in sharpening chisels, the surface gets a dark metallic glaze, and the stone will not then bite the steel. To remove this glaze the stone was ''whetted'' or sharpened (both terms were used) by rubbing it with sand and water, the rubbing medium being a piece of stone harder . . . and of coarser grain.|{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 173.}}}} '''4.''' To cut with a knife.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. VI., ii. 1. 34.}}}} '''To whet one’s whistle†.''' Same as ''to wet one’s whistle'' (confusion of ''wet'' and ''whet''). See ''whistle.'' {{smaller block|Give the boy some drink there! Piper, ''Whet your whistle.'' ''Fletcher'', Beggars’ Bush, iii. 1. Let ’s e’en say grace, and turn to the fire, drink the other cup to ''whet our whistles'', and so sing away all sad thoughts. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 86.}}}} '''whet''' (hwet), ''n.''   [< ''whet'', ''v.'']   The act of sharpening by friction; hence, something that provokes or stimulates; especially, something that whets the appetite, as a dram. {{smaller block|You are cloy’d with the Preparative, and what you mean for a ''Whet'' turns the Edge of your puny Stomachs. {{right|''Congreve'', Old Batchelor, i. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|He had assisted at four hundred bowls of punch, not to mention sips, drams, and ''whets'' without number. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator.}}}} {{smaller block|Mr. Mayor gives a ''whet'' [a light luncheon] to-day after church, when he hopes you will attend. {{right|Quoted in ''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 55.}}}} '''whether'''1 (hweᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''a.'' and ''pron.''   [Formerly also contr. ''wher'', ''where''; < ME. ''whether'', ''whather'', ''whæther'', ''wether'', ''wather'', ''hwether'', ''hwather'', ''qwether'', also contr. ''wher'', < AS. ''hwæther'', ''hwether'' = OS. ''hwethar'', ''hueder'' = OFries. ''hweder'', ''hoder'' = MLG. ''weder'', ''wedder'', LG. ''wedder'', ''weer'' = OHG. ''hwedar'', ''huedar'', ''wedar'', which of two, MHG. G. ''weder'' = Icel. ''hvadharr'', contr. ''hvārr'', ''hvorr'' = Goth. ''hwathar'', which (of two); = OBulg. Russ. ''kotoruiĭ'', which, = L. ''uter'' (for *''cuter'') = Gr. κότερος, πότερος = Skt. ''katara'', which (of two); with compar. suffix ''-ther'' (''-der'', ''-ter'', etc.), from the base ''hwa'' of the pron. ''who'': see ''who'', and cf. ''what''1, etc. Cf. ''either''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''A.''' ''interrog.'' Which (of two)? which one? '''B.''' ''rel.'' (always in compound relative use, or with the antecedent implied, not expressed). Which (of two, or, less exactly, of more than two). {{smaller block|When the father him bethought, And sighe [saw] to ''whether'' side it drough. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|I woulde gladly knowe in ''whether'' booke you haue read moste, which is to wit, in Vegetius, which entreateth of matters of wars, or in S. Augustine his boke of Christiã doctrine. {{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 238.}}}} {{smaller block|But to ''whether'' side fortune would have been partial could not be determined. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.}}}} '''II.''' ''pron.'' '''A.''' ''interrog.'' Which (of two, or of the two)? which one (of two)? {{smaller block|''Whether'' of them [the, R. V.] twain did the will of his father? {{right|Mat. xxi. 31.}}}} '''B.''' ''rel.'' Which (of two); which one (of two); also, more indefinitely, whichever. {{smaller block|Well, I will hear, or sleep, I care not ''whether.'' {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Captain, ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|It may be a question among men of noble sentiments, ''whether'' of these unfortunate persons had the greater soul. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|“Chese now,” quod she, “oon of thise thinges tweye . . . Now chese your selven ''whether'' that you liketh.” {{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 371.}}}} {{smaller block|Bothe ʒonge & oolde, ''whethir'' ʒe be, In cristis name good cheer ʒe make. {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 32.}}}} {{smaller block|To waxen or to wonien, ''whether'' God lyketh. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), viii. 59.}}}} '''whether'''1 (hweᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''whether'', ''wheder'', ''wether'', ''hwether'', contr. ''wher'', ''wer'', < AS. ''hwæther'', ''hwether'' = OS. ''hwethar'' = OFries. ''hweder'' = MLG. ''weder'', ''wedder'' = OHG. ''hwedar'', ''wedar'', MHG. G. ''weder'' = Icel. ''hvārt'', whether; orig. neut. of the pron. ''whether'': see ''whether'', ''a.'' and ''pron.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' '''1.''' Introducing the first of two direct (alternative) questions, the second being introduced by ''or'' (literally, which of these two things [is true]?). {{smaller block|''Whether'' is Herod, ''or'' that Youngling, King? {{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iii. 161.}}}} '''2†.''' Introducing a single direct question, the alternative being unexpressed, and sometimes only dimly implied. {{smaller block|''Whether'' is not this the sone of a carpenter? ''Whether'' his modir be not seid [called] Marie? {{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xiii. 55.}}}} {{smaller block|Well then, if God will not allow a king too much, ''whether'' will he allow a subject too much? {{right|''Latimer'', 1st Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}} {{smaller block|What authoritye thinke you meete to be given him? ''whether'' will ye allowe him to protecte, to safe conducte, and to have marshall lawe as they are accustomed? {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' '''1.''' Introducing the first of two (or more) alternatives, the second being introduced by ''or'' (or ''or whether''). {{smaller block|''Whether'' ȝe ben aposid of princes or of prestis of the lawe, For to answere hem haue ȝe no doute. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), xi. 289.}}}} {{smaller block|''Whether'' the tyranny be in his place ''Or'' in his eminence that fills it up. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 167.}}}} {{smaller block|Thou shalt speak my words unto them, ''whether'' they will hear ''or whether'' they will forbear. {{right|Ezek. ii. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|But ''whether'' thus these things, ''or whether'' not; ''Whether'' the sun, predominant in heaven, Rise on the earth, ''or'' earth rise on the sun; . . . Solicit not thy thoughts with matters hid. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 159.}}}} {{smaller block|The Moors, ''whether'' wounded ''or'' slain, were thrown headlong without the walls. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 54.}}}} {{smaller block|Laws may be received as indicating the dispositions of the ruler, ''whether'' for good ''or'' for evil. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 26.}}}} {{smaller block|There are moments in life when the lip and the eye Try the question of ''whether'' to smile ''or'' to cry. {{right|''Whittier'', The Quaker Alumni.}}}} {{smaller block|So long as men had slender means, ''whether'' of keeping out cold ''or'' checkmating it with artificial heat, Winter was an unwelcome guest, especially in the country. {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 30.}}}}
